pos: n. (proper name; a Korhite who joined David at Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew Yo'ezer, the LORD is help, from Yah and 'ezer, help.
biblical_def: Joezer is one of the Korhites who came to David at Ziklag. “Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites” (1 Chronicles 12:6). They were numbered among those who came “while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war” (1 Chronicles 12:1). The Korhites descended from Korah, who rebelled against Moses and was swallowed by the earth. Yet “Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not” (Numbers 26:11). Their line was spared, and in later generations the sons of Korah wrote psalms and kept the doors of the house of God: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psalm 84:10). Joezer, the LORD is help, came from a family that owed its very existence to God's mercy, and he gave his strength to God's anointed. The son of a rebel's house became a helper of the true king.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Jeroham of Gedor who joined David)
etymology: Hebrew Yo'elah, perhaps may he avail or let him help; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Joelah is one of the two sons of Jeroham of Gedor who came to David at Ziklag. “And Joelah, and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor” (1 Chronicles 12:7). They appear in the list of men who joined David while he hid from Saul, “among the mighty men, helpers of the war” (1 Chronicles 12:1). They were “armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow” (1 Chronicles 12:2), a skill prized among the Benjamites. Gedor may be the Benjamite town or the Judahite one; Scripture does not say. What it does record is that these men came early, when David was an outlaw, and their faithfulness was remembered when he was crowned. The chapter ends at Hebron: “All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel” (1 Chronicles 12:38). Joelah's loyalty began at Ziklag and ended at the throne.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, and a captain of Manasseh who joined David)
etymology: Hebrew Tsilletay, shadow of the LORD or shady, from tsel, shadow.
biblical_def: Zilthai is the name of two men in Chronicles. The first is a Benjamite in the house of Shimhi: “And Elienai, and Zilthai, and Eliel” (1 Chronicles 8:20), followed by “Adaiah, and Beraiah, and Shimrath, the sons of Shimhi” (1 Chronicles 8:21). The second is a captain of Manasseh who joined David on the eve of Saul's last battle: “As he went to Ziklag, there fell to him of Manasseh, Adnah, and Jozabad, and Jediael, and Michael, and Jozabad, and Elihu, and Zilthai, captains of the thousands that were of Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 12:20). “And they helped David against the band of the rovers: for they were all mighty men of valour, and were captains in the host” (1 Chronicles 12:21). The Manassite captains defected as David returned from the Philistine camp, just before Saul died on Gilboa. Zilthai's name may mean shadow of the LORD, recalling the refuge of the psalms. He came to the shadow of God's anointed at the turning of the kingdom.

pos: n. (proper name; a servant who killed king Joash; called Zabad in Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Yozakar, the LORD remembers, from Yah and zakar, to remember.
biblical_def: Jozachar is one of the two servants who murdered Joash, king of Judah. “For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David: and Amaziah his son reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 12:21). Chronicles calls him Zabad and gives the cause: “his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed” (2 Chronicles 24:25). “Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith a Moabitess” (2 Chronicles 24:26). Joash had killed Zechariah, the son of the priest who saved and raised him; “Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him” (2 Chronicles 24:22). Zechariah died saying, “The LORD look upon it, and require it.” Jozachar's name means the LORD remembers, and in him the LORD remembered. The murder was sin, and Amaziah later executed the assassins; yet God used it to require the blood of His prophet.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor in the line of Gad)
biblical_def: Jaroah is a Gadite named in the genealogy of Abihail. “These are the children of Abihail the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz” (1 Chronicles 5:14). The Gadites “dwelt in Gilead in Bashan, and in her towns” (1 Chronicles 5:16), east of Jordan, and their genealogies were recorded “in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel” (1 Chronicles 5:17). The men of this line went to war with the Hagarites and won, “for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him” (1 Chronicles 5:20). Jaroah's name means moon. He stands in a chain of seven generations that the Chronicler kept for a people returned from exile, so they would know that God had not forgotten the tribes beyond Jordan.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor in the line of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Yeshishay, aged, venerable, from yashish, an old man.
biblical_def: Jeshishai is a Gadite ancestor in the line of Abihail. “These are the children of Abihail the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz” (1 Chronicles 5:14). His name means aged or venerable. The tribe dwelt east of Jordan, and “the children of Gad dwelt over against them, in the land of Bashan unto Salchah” (1 Chronicles 5:11). The Gadites joined Reuben and Manasseh in war, “valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war” (1 Chronicles 5:18), and they prevailed because they trusted God. But the end of the chapter is the end of their story: “they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land” (1 Chronicles 5:25). The venerable name of an ancestor did not keep his descendants faithful. Each generation must seek the LORD.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor in the line of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Yachdo, his union or together, from yachad, together, unitedly.
biblical_def: Jahdo is a Gadite ancestor named in the line of Abihail, the son of Buz. “These are the children of Abihail the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz” (1 Chronicles 5:14). His name means together, and the chapter that preserves it tells of the tribes east of Jordan acting together. Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh went out together to war, and “they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand” (1 Chronicles 5:20). “For there fell down many slain, because the war was of God. And they dwelt in their steads until the captivity” (1 Chronicles 5:22). Then they went into captivity together as well, when “the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria” (1 Chronicles 5:26). A people united in victory may be united in apostasy. Jahdo's name is a reminder that unity is good only when it is unity in the truth.

pos: n. (proper name; a Gadite chief of a father's house)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'kan, troubled or afflicting, from a root related to 'akar, to trouble.
biblical_def: Jachan is one of seven Gadite brethren named among the heads of their fathers' houses. “And their brethren of the house of their fathers were, Michael, and Meshullam, and Sheba, and Jorai, and Jachan, and Zia, and Heber, seven” (1 Chronicles 5:13). The chiefs of Gad are listed just before: “Joel the chief, and Shapham the next, and Jaanai, and Shaphat in Bashan” (1 Chronicles 5:12). The tribe settled in Bashan and Gilead, rich pastureland east of Jordan, which their fathers had asked of Moses for their cattle. They “dwelt in Gilead in Bashan, and in her towns” (1 Chronicles 5:16). Seven brothers, seven heads of houses, are named and nothing more is said of any of them. Jachan's name may mean troubled. The tribe's prosperity east of Jordan proved a snare; separated from the sanctuary by the river and surrounded by the nations, Gad drifted into the worship of the gods of the land and was among the first carried away by Assyria.

pos: n. (proper name; a Gadite chief of a father's house)
etymology: Hebrew Yoray, the LORD teaches or whom the LORD teaches, from yarah, to teach.
biblical_def: Jorai is one of the seven brethren who headed houses of the tribe of Gad. “And their brethren of the house of their fathers were, Michael, and Meshullam, and Sheba, and Jorai, and Jachan, and Zia, and Heber, seven” (1 Chronicles 5:13). His name may mean the LORD teaches. The Gadites were “reckoned by genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel” (1 Chronicles 5:17), during the prosperous years before the fall of the north. Those years ended in judgment. “And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them” (1 Chronicles 5:25), and God sent Assyria to carry them “unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day” (1 Chronicles 5:26). A name that confessed the LORD as teacher stood in a tribe that would not be taught. The Chronicler preserved it so that the returned exiles would learn what Gad would not.

pos: n. (proper name; a Gadite chief of a father's house)
etymology: Hebrew Zia', motion or trembling, from zua', to tremble, to move.
biblical_def: Zia is one of the seven Gadite brethren who headed houses of their fathers. “And their brethren of the house of their fathers were, Michael, and Meshullam, and Sheba, and Jorai, and Jachan, and Zia, and Heber, seven” (1 Chronicles 5:13). His name may mean trembling. Gad was a warrior tribe; Moses had blessed it, “he dwelleth as a lion,” and the Gadites who later joined David were men “whose faces were like the faces of lions” (1 Chronicles 12:8). The men of Zia's generation went out with Reuben and Manasseh, “valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war” (1 Chronicles 5:18), and won because “the war was of God” (1 Chronicles 5:22). Valor is a gift of God, and so is victory; neither is a substitute for faithfulness. The same chapter that records Gad's valor records its captivity. Zia, one name in seven, belongs to a tribe whose strength could not save it once it forsook the LORD.

corruption_summary: Strength is trusted for security; the valiant men of Gad, Zia's brethren, prevailed only because the war was of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers skip the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as dead lists. The Chronicler wrote them for a people returned from exile who needed to know who they were and why they had been scattered. The names of Gad are framed by a victory won through trust and a captivity earned by idolatry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God who fights for His people when they trust Him also removes them when they forsake Him. The Gadites “cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him” (1 Chronicles 5:20); their sons went a whoring after other gods and were carried away.
